title: FPGA Design
description: What an FPGA contains, how the design flow turns RTL into a bitstream, how clocks and constraints work, and when an FPGA or an ASIC is the better choice.

questions.explanation: Simulation gives quick iteration and full visibility of signals.

lessons.title: Inside an FPGA: LUTs, Flip-Flops and Routing
objectives: Explain how a LUT implements any logic function
List the main resources in an FPGA
lessons.body:
An FPGA is a chip whose logic and wiring are configured after manufacturing. Its basic logic element is the look-up table (LUT). A 4-input LUT is a tiny memory with 16 one-bit cells: the four inputs form an address and the stored bit at that address is the output. Loading different bits makes the LUT behave as any 4-input function, such as AND, XOR or a custom truth table.

Each LUT is usually paired with a flip-flop so it can produce a registered output. Groups of these cells form configurable logic blocks. Around them the chip has programmable routing wires and switches, input/output blocks, and dedicated resources such as block RAM and DSP blocks for multiplication.

The exact LUT size, block layout and resource counts differ by vendor and device family, so always check the datasheet of your board. In many designs the delay of the routing wires is a large part of the total path delay.

definitions.meaning: Look-up table: a small memory whose contents define a logic function.
Configurable logic block: a group of LUTs and flip-flops.
Programmable wires and switches that connect logic blocks.

lessons.exampleNote: Only in = 1111 selects bit 15. Setting just that bit gives a 4-input AND; the pattern 6996 hex gives odd parity (4-input XOR).
lessons.diagram:
in[3:0] --> [ 16 x 1-bit ] --> out
             [  memory    ]
  address = in, data = stored bit
         |
         v
  [ D flip-flop ] --> registered out
mistakes: Thinking an FPGA runs software: it is configured hardware, not a processor running code.
Ignoring routing delay when estimating speed: wires add significant delay.
Assuming every FPGA has the same resources: check the specific device.

practice.q: How many truth-table bits does a 4-input LUT store?
What pairs with a LUT to give registered outputs?
practice.a: A flip-flop in the same logic cell.

exercises: Run the LUT demo and read the AND and XOR tables.
Compute the 16-bit configuration for a 4-input OR.
summary: A LUT is a small configurable memory.
LUT + flip-flop is the basic logic cell.
Routing, block RAM and DSP blocks complete the device.

lessons.title: From RTL to Bitstream
objectives: List the steps of the FPGA flow
Say what synthesis and place-and-route produce
lessons.body:
The FPGA flow turns your HDL into a configuration file for the chip. First you write RTL and simulate it to check behaviour. Synthesis converts the RTL into a netlist of generic gates and registers, then maps it onto the device's LUTs and flip-flops.

Implementation follows. Placement chooses which physical logic cell holds each part of the netlist, and routing selects the wires and switches that connect them. The tool then reports timing and resource usage, so you can see whether the design meets its clock and how much of the device it uses.

Finally the tool generates a bitstream, the file that sets every LUT bit and routing switch, and you program it into the FPGA through a cable or from flash. If timing fails, you change the RTL or the constraints and run the flow again.

definitions.meaning: Converting RTL into a netlist of logic mapped to device resources.
Choosing physical locations for logic and the wires between them.
The configuration file loaded into the FPGA.
How much of the device's LUTs, flip-flops and memory the design uses.

lessons.diagram:
RTL + testbench
       |  simulate
       v
   Synthesis -> netlist
       v
  Place and route
       v
  Timing / utilization reports
       v
  Bitstream -> program the FPGA
mistakes: Skipping simulation and debugging on the board: simulation is much faster to iterate.
Ignoring timing reports: a design that fails timing may work only sometimes.
Treating warnings as noise: unconnected or inferred-latch warnings point to real bugs.

practice.a: A netlist mapped to the device's resources.

practice.q: What is loaded into the FPGA?

exercises: Write the flow steps in order from memory.
In HDL Studio compile and run a design: which flow step does that correspond to?
summary: Simulate first, then synthesize, place, route and generate a bitstream.

lessons.title: Clocks and Constraints
objectives: Prefer clock enables to derived clocks
lessons.body:
Constraints tell the tools what your design needs. Pin constraints map each top-level port to a physical pin. Timing constraints state the clock period, for example a 100 MHz clock has a 10 ns period, so the tools know which paths must be fast enough.

When you need a slower rate, avoid creating new clocks from logic outputs where you can. A common safer style is to keep one clock and use a counter to create an enable pulse, so the registers only act every Nth cycle. Dedicated clock-management blocks such as PLLs are used when a genuinely different frequency is needed.

A signal that crosses between two unrelated clocks needs special synchronisation. Without it, a flip-flop can sample during a change and go metastable. The demo is a simple divide-by-4 output built with a counter.

definitions.meaning: A requirement given to the tools, such as pin location or clock period.
A signal that lets registers act only on selected clock cycles.
A group of registers driven by the same clock.
An undefined flip-flop state caused by sampling during a change.

lessons.example:
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) begin c <= 0; slow <= 0; end
  else begin
    c <= c + 1;
    if (c == 1) begin slow <= ~slow; c <= 0; end
  end
end
lessons.exampleNote: slow toggles every second clock cycle, so one full period of slow lasts four cycles of clk.
mistakes: Using a logic output as a clock without need: prefer an enable on the fast clock.
Forgetting to constrain the clock: timing results are meaningless without it.
Crossing clock domains with a single wire: add a synchroniser.

practice.q: What is the period of a 100 MHz clock?
Why prefer a clock enable to a derived clock?
practice.a: It keeps one clock domain and simplifies timing.

exercises: Run the demo and read the slow clock pattern.
Change the counter to divide by 8.
summary: Constraints give pin locations and clock periods.

lessons.title: FPGA or ASIC?
objectives: Compare FPGAs and ASICs on cost, speed, power and flexibility
Pick a sensible target for a given project
lessons.body:
An ASIC is a chip designed for one purpose and manufactured with custom masks. An FPGA is a standard chip that you configure.

In general, an ASIC has a high one-time engineering cost (NRE) but a low cost per chip at high volume, and it can reach higher speed and lower power for a given function. An FPGA has no mask cost, can be reprogrammed in the field, and gets a design running quickly, but each unit costs more and the same function usually runs slower and uses more power.

That is why FPGAs are popular for prototypes, low-volume products and designs that must change, while very high-volume products often use ASICs. Many ASIC projects first prototype on an FPGA. These are general tendencies, and the real answer depends on volume, schedule and requirements.

definitions.meaning: Application-specific integrated circuit built for one purpose.
Non-recurring engineering cost paid once to design and make the chip.
An early working version used to test ideas.
Able to change its function by loading a new configuration.

lessons.diagram:
Cost per chip
  ^
  | FPGA ----------------
  |
  |  ASIC ..... (after NRE)
  +--------------------> volume
  (simplified, not to scale)
mistakes: Saying FPGAs are always slower: they are slower for the same function in general, not in every case.
Ignoring NRE: low per-chip cost needs high volume to pay off.
Choosing ASIC for a design that will change often.

practice.q: Which one has mask cost, FPGA or ASIC?
Why prototype an ASIC on an FPGA?
practice.a: To test behaviour early without paying for masks.

exercises: List three products that suit an FPGA and three that suit an ASIC.
summary: ASIC: high NRE, low unit cost at volume, best speed/power.
FPGA: no NRE, flexible, quicker to start.
Choose by volume, schedule and flexibility.
